item.description: From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy. Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration. Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s […]

item.title: NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland
item.description: A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Transit, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations. Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy […]

item.description: Registration is open for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, a two-day global event on Saturday, Nov. 14 and Sunday, Nov. 15, where teams work to create solutions inspired by NASA’s most ambitious exploration goals and making use of the agency’s free and open data. The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, […]

item.description: NASA has selected 12 U.S. institutions to receive $12 million to accelerate academic research and technology development in support of the agency’s priorities for exploring the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Through NASA’s Minority University Research and Education Project (MUREP) Space Technology Artemis Research (M‑STAR) initiative, selected institutions will each receive up to $1 million […]

item.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance
item.description: NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the Moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the Moon’s surface. Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected. In particular, NASA measured whether the thermal protection […]

item.title: Chandra Finds Possible Origin of ‘Treble Clef’ Waves
item.description: A formation of radio waves looks remarkably like a treble clef in this Oct. 14, 2026, image from NASA’s Chandra X-Ray Observatory. Researchers used Chandra to find that the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters. Read more about this discovery. […]

item.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
item.description: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

item.title: Arctic sea ice hits another troubling low in 2026
item.description: Arctic sea ice is shrinking in both winter and summer, with satellite records revealing that the region's remaining ice is becoming thinner, younger, and more vulnerable to melting. Despite a recent slowdown in summer losses, scientists warn that the Arctic could experience a nearly ice-free summer before 2050.

item.title: Eating late at night linked to up to 30% higher risk of liver disease
item.description: Eating late at night could be putting your liver at risk, according to a large study led by Oregon Health & Science University. Researchers analyzed data from nearly 200,000 people and found that those who regularly ate after dinner or around bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, including fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.

item.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
item.description: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes.

item.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
item.description: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.

item.title: Strokes have nearly doubled among younger adults, and scientists aren't sure why
item.description: Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades. Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

item.title: Ozempic and Wegovy linked to rare risk of sudden vision loss
item.description: Popular diabetes and weight loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy have been linked to a slightly increased risk of a rare condition that can cause sudden, potentially permanent vision loss. Although the risk remains very low, Rutgers researchers say the findings warrant attention as millions of people turn to GLP-1 medications.

item.title: Fires Arrive in the Amazon Rainforest
item.description: During El Niño, a cascade of fires across the tropics begins in equatorial Asia and continues in the central and eastern Amazon.

item.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
item.description: A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance.

item.title: Is AI eroding PhD students’ critical thinking and analysis skills?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03178-w An expert panel debates the impact of artificial intelligence on doctoral programmes.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03329-z Governments have voted to abolish the leap second immediately and replace it with a leap hour.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03238-1 Solitary primates spend energy and time travelling to patches of forest for get-togethers.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03233-6 Programmer whose forward-thinking and reliable code helped to save the Apollo 11 mission.

item.title: ArXiv versus AI slop: will capping preprint submissions work?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03194-w Major preprint platform tightens its rules to curb a surge of submissions, including those generated by artificial-intelligence tools.

item.title: Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
item.description: A groundbreaking study suggests that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization, far more than previously believed. Researchers estimate that 93% of this population was lost within 73 years, revealing a demographic catastrophe on a scale that dramatically changes our understanding of Australian history.

item.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
item.description: A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters.

item.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
item.description: A major study found that several cancers are rising faster among younger adults in England, even as smoking, diet, and other established risk factors have generally improved. Excess weight explains only part of the increase, leaving scientists searching for other possible causes, including changes in the gut microbiome and early-life exposures.

item.title: NASA to Host News Conference Previewing US Spacewalks 100, 101
item.description: NASA will preview two upcoming spacewalks to complete solar array installation and power augmentation of the International Space Station during a news conference at 2 p.m. EDT, Tuesday, Oct. 20, from NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA will stream the event through a variety of platforms. Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live NASA participants […]

Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station. The Earth-to-space call will begin at 12:30 p.m. EDT Friday, Oct. 16, […]

item.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
item.description: Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.

item.title: Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
item.description: Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.

item.title: The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
item.description: Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more.

item.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
item.description: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

item.title: Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
item.description: Scientists may have solved a long-standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different, using samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings suggest that uneven heating from Earth's gravitational pull drove enormous flows of ancient magma, creating the dramatically different lunar landscapes we see today.

item.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
item.description: Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research.

item.title: Gigantic prehistoric snake discovered in India may have been one of the largest ever
item.description: A massive prehistoric snake discovered in India may have rivaled the largest snake ever known. Called Vasuki indicus, the 47-million-year-old giant could have reached up to 50 feet long, making it comparable to the legendary Titanoboa. Scientists believe its enormous body made it a slow-moving ambush predator, similar to a modern anaconda.

item.title: New knee arthritis treatment delivers lasting pain relief without surgery
item.description: A promising new treatment for knee arthritis uses tiny, dissolvable particles to block abnormal blood vessels, easing inflammation and pain without joint replacement surgery. In a study of 194 patients, 80% experienced clinically meaningful pain relief lasting at least 12 months.

item.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
item.description: A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.

item.title: A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
item.description: Astronomers have discovered that a scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away shares a striking chemical similarity with its host star, providing the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about planet formation. The breakthrough could help scientists predict what distant rocky planets are made of and identify worlds with conditions favorable for life.

item.title: AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
item.description: Scientists used artificial intelligence to uncover nearly 10,000 chemical reactions involved in transforming carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals, revealing crucial pathways that traditional models had missed. The discovery dramatically improved predictions of CO2 conversion and uncovered a surprising hydrogen reaction that could inspire more efficient catalysts.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03307-5 Analysis suggests number of protected areas is hugely underestimated but biodiversity is still in peril — plus, a huge study looking at the health effects of brown fat.

item.title: Lay of the land: terrestrial conservation efforts cover a wider area than thought
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03081-4 Governments around the world have pledged to conserve 30% of the terrestrial realm by 2030, but official data suggest that the target is barely halfway to being met. A combined global and national-level data set now shows that up to 27% of land area is conserved, but gaps in ecological representation remain.

item.title: Will my lack of country-specific grants limit my chances of employment abroad?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02442-3 A researcher in Latin America seeks advice on the best way to present themselves when applying for faculty positions in Europe and North America.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03204-x These nations are making their distinct mark in the field through specialization and collaboration.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03247-0 A tool called IdeaLens helps to judge whether concepts — rather than just writing — in scientific papers are AI-generated.

item.title: Some Jurassic period birds were flightless
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02645-8 The fossil discovery of an early avian ancestor in China reveals that flightless birds lived alongside the known flying species.

item.title: Large blind test of methane-detecting satellites lends credibility to emissions data
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03075-2 Twelve methane-sensing satellites were tested for their accuracy in measuring controlled-release events in the Arizona desert over a year-long blind test. Many were found to detect and quantify releases accurately, with instruments purpose-built for methane sensing performing best.

item.title: Daily briefing: China’s extraordinary rise in science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03322-6 Explore China’s efforts to grow its scientific and technological might. Plus, how butterflies trick the eye and what could be the oldest shipwreck ever found.

item.title: China’s AI research is booming: what it’s like to be on the front line
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03223-8 China trains more AI talent than any other country. Nature spoke to analysts and scientists about how AI research there compares to the United States.

item.title: Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03219-4 Appeals for extra money are failing. Fundamental changes are needed to safeguard the planet for future generations.

item.title: ‘Incredible’: bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03266-x A coral fragment can form a tissue bridge with a dying counterpart — and provide it with crucial microalgae.

item.title: Alveolar stem cells go beyond making gas-exchange cells to repair damaged airways
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03085-0 Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are the stem cells of the lung’s air sacs and are responsible for maintaining alveolar structure and gas exchange. A study that tracked AT2 cells shows that, after injury to the airway, they can also migrate between lung compartments and become bronchiolar cells to help repair damaged airways.

item.title: Hydrogels and MRI: meet three biomedical engineers reshaping health care
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03205-w Researchers are making great advances across medical disciplines, using a wide range of tools and processes.

item.title: How early tetrapods got their neck
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03061-8 As fish evolved into four-limbed creatures, their skull separated from their shoulders to form a neck. Now we learn that this early neck was surprisingly rigid.

item.title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11239-3 Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs

item.title: Overlooked brown fat in our bodies linked to wide range of health benefits
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03302-w Massive study of more than 100,000 people finds surprise connection between ‘good’ body fat and improved mental health.

item.title: Smartwatch health data are piling up. How can doctors keep pace?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03203-y To harness the full value of wearable devices for monitoring and diagnosing medical conditions, protocols must be established.

item.title: China’s extraordinary rise in science and how it will change the world
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03222-9 The nation is on a trajectory to lead the world in science, a development that will reshape technological advancement, innovation and the balance of global power.

item.title: Evidence for multi-Li<sup>+</sup> clustering in lithium-ion battery electrolytes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11138-7 Machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations, spectroscopy, electrochemical data and quantum-chemical calculations reveal previously unstudied multi-lithium-ion complexes without bound anions, improving understanding of lithium-ion-battery functionality at the atomic level.

item.title: Global conservation area coverage substantially exceeds current estimates
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11157-4 A globally representative sample of 25 countries and territories indicates that conservation areas cover 26.81% of the land, much closer to the 30% by 2030 target than officially reported.

item.title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11176-1 A tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells.

item.title: Elp1 is required for myeloid differentiation and brain repopulation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11112-3 Primary cultured haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells are used to analyse the molecular mechanisms of brain myeloid differentiation, and this platform enabled the identification of elongation factor ELP1 as an important regulator of this process.

item.title: Modelling mouse embryogenesis from chemically induced totipotent stem cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11164-5 A mouse embryo model derived from chemically induced totipotent-like stem cells progresses through key developmental milestones, including gastrulation, embryonic axis formation, haematopoiesis and early organogenesis.

item.title: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11065-7 The mechanical properties of medium-entropy alloys at 20 K show a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition.

item.title: Parity-dependent coupling of molecular spin chains to a superconductor
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11117-y Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy shows that the fractional spin-1/2 end states of molecular Haldane chains couple differently to a superconducting condensate depending on whether the chain contains an even or odd number of spin-1 triangulene units.

item.title: Capillary-selective vasodilation through myosin inhibition halts ischaemic cascades
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11171-6 R(+)2501 reverses capillary no-reflow by relaxing pericytes, restoring microvascular perfusion and improving survival in animal models of myocardial infarction and acute kidney injury.

item.title: Evaluating space-based methane detection through a one-year blind test
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11115-0 A year-long single-blind study shows that multiple satellites can accurately detect and quantify methane point-source emissions.

item.title: De novo design of cysteine proteases
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11143-w De novo-designed enzymes use an activated cysteine nucleophile to hydrolyse polypeptide backbones in a sequence-dependent manner.

item.title: Computational design of metalloproteases
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11167-2 RFdiffusion methods are used to de novo design proteins with water-activating zinc-based active sites adjacent to a peptide substrate binding pocket, yielding highly active, programmable proteases with potential applications in therapeutics, biotechnology and bioremediation.

item.title: Divergent genomic evolution in astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11150-x Longitudinal genomic analyses in patients with astrocytoma or oligodendrioglioma suggest that these two types of tumour differ in the mechanisms by which they become resistant to treatment, with astrocytomas accumulating copy-number alterations and chromosomal instability markers but oligodendrogliomas acquiring new driver mutations.

item.title: Rh<sup>3+</sup> stabilized in KRh@MFI catalyses regioselective hydroformylation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11136-9 DFT investigations combined with spectroscopic and catalytic studies of disrupted subnanometric Rh2O3 clusters show that Rh+ centres in a zeolite-based catalyst are blocked with N-containing molecules, whereas Rh3+ sites are stabilized, allowing hydroformylation reactions with enhanced regioselectivity and efficiency.

item.title: Targeted stimulation of motor cortex ensembles drives learned movements
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11174-3 Optogenetic stimulation of motor-cortex neuron ensembles shows that precisely timed activity in the primary motor cortex can generate learned neural patterns and movements, demonstrating an active role in skilled motor control.

item.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11162-7 Artificial intelligence-enabled quantification and analyses of brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity uncover links between BAT and a healthier metabolic profile along with lower rates of psychiatric disease, and can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate this tissue in humans.

item.title: Early tetrapod neck mobility modelled using an extant analogue
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11158-3 Biomechanical analysis of several early tetrapods using sturgeon as an analogue revealed that early tetrapods had limited neck mobility despite separation of the head and shoulders.

item.title: Intrinsic physicochemical activity at microplastic–water interfaces
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11141-y Commodity microplastics exhibit intrinsic physicochemical activity at water interfaces, manifested by spontaneous generation of reactive oxygen species, challenging the prevailing paradigm of plastic inertness, with implications for human health and the environment.

item.title: Hidden reaction pathways inform additive engineering for perovskite LEDs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11120-3 Resolution and control of the hidden solution-phase chemistry of 5-aminovaleric acid added to perovskite precursor solutions is described for producing films with a near-unity mean peak photoluminescence quantum yield and near-infrared perovskite LEDs with enhanced external quantum efficiencies.

item.title: Clasping folds enable superior elastic strength of graphene films
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11109-y Two-dimensional graphene films with unusual folded surfaces are synthesized through a modular assembly strategy and show enhanced strength, toughness and elastic strain owing to stress distribution between interlayer folds.

item.title: Wave coarsening drives time crystallization in mechatronic metamaterials
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11163-6 Wave coarsening in active elastic media is a phenomenon in which vibrations spontaneously increase in wavelength, period and amplitude before forming a globally synchronized time crystal.

item.title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11159-2 Long-term live imaging of adult mouse ear skin reveals sex-specific differences in the clonal dynamics of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cells during homeostasis.

item.title: Interhemispheric monsoon dynamics over the past 450,000 years
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11166-3 A 450 ka Andean speleothem record shows Southern and Northern Hemisphere monsoons generally vary out of phase, but occasionally synchronize during rapid climate change and glacial terminations.

item.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11119-w A regulatory sequence code for neuronal microexons reveals genetic variants predicted to alter their splicing in individuals with autism.

item.title: Educational intervention can rewire village social networks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11154-7 A randomized controlled trial involving a health-education intervention in rural villages in Honduras shows that the intervention changed social network connections, including not only health-related connections but also friendships and financial ties.

item.title: Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11126-x The AI framework probabilistic bias correction is shown to correct weather forecast errors 2 to 6 weeks ahead and boost forecast skill, making it promising for improved extreme-weather prediction.

item.title: Jurassic flightless bird reveals early ecological diversity of avialans
item.description: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z A fossil bird from the Upper Jurassic Zhenghe Fauna of southeastern China contemporary with Archaeopteryx and that clearly could not fly sheds new light on the ecological diversification of early-diverging avialans.

item.title: 210-million-year-old dinosaur discovery reveals a lost world in Africa
item.description: A newly identified 210-million-year-old dinosaur from Zimbabwe is helping scientists uncover a surprisingly distinct prehistoric ecosystem. The discovery suggests that ancient climate differences may have separated dinosaur populations across southern Africa, leading to unique species that challenge previous assumptions about their evolution.

item.title: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
item.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising paradox in how our cells age
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the body's cellular recycling system behaves very differently during aging than previously believed, with higher activity sometimes linked to worse physical health. A small study suggests that even gentle exercise could help restore more youthful cellular recycling patterns in older adults.

item.title: This tiny jurassic predator helped pave the way for the human brain
item.description: A 165-million-year-old fossil has revealed an extraordinary Jurassic predator that may help explain how mammals developed one of their most important evolutionary advantages. Although only 20 inches long, Megacauda sungei was a heavyweight among early mammal relatives, swimming through ancient waterways and hunting prey with specialized teeth. Its advanced swallowing anatomy reveals an early step toward the ability to safely nurse on milk, a key development in mammalian evolution.

item.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
item.description: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

item.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
item.description: Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.

item.title: The secret to handling stress better may start at breakfast
item.description: Your daily routine could have a bigger impact on your ability to handle stress than you realize. A Binghamton University study of approximately 400 college students found that eating breakfast regularly, exercising, sleeping well, and taking fish oil were associated with greater psychological flexibility, which helps people adapt to stressful situations. Poor sleep and unhealthy eating habits, meanwhile, were linked to lower flexibility and resilience.

item.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.

item.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.

item.title: Scientists just gave the powerhouses of our cells a high-tech upgrade
item.description: Scientists have created a new coating for mitochondria that preserves their ability to produce energy, potentially opening the door to new treatments for diseases involving these tiny cellular powerhouses. The technology could one day help transfer healthy mitochondria into damaged cells, although its effectiveness in transplantation remains unproven.

item.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
item.description: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

item.title: Scientists find a hidden problem with endless smartphone scrolling
item.description: Excessive smartphone use may be taking a hidden toll on the brain and body, with heavy scrolling linked to poorer memory, reduced attention, disrupted sleep, and potential balance problems. Researchers found that weak self-control and fear of missing out, rather than personality alone, are key factors behind problematic phone use.

item.title: Your gut bacteria could be changing how many calories you absorb
item.description: Scientists have developed a model showing that gut bacteria play a surprisingly important role in how many calories we absorb, meaning food labels may not tell the full story. In a controlled study, people eating a high-fiber diet absorbed about 116 fewer calories per day than those eating a typical Western diet, without feeling hungrier.

item.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
item.description: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

item.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
item.description: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

item.title: Popular weight loss drugs linked to a surprising fingernail problem
item.description: Popular GLP-1 weight loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Wegovy, have been linked to unexpectedly high rates of nail detachment, hair loss, and scalp inflammation, with some problems occurring several times more frequently among users. Researchers found that weight loss alone could not fully explain the differences, suggesting there may be more to these overlooked symptoms.

item.title: Scientists find hidden driver of aging and a simple amino acid that fights memory loss in mice
item.description: Scientists discovered that declining levels of a protein called Menin may help drive aging, and restoring it in older mice reversed several age-related changes in just 30 days. Even more surprisingly, supplementing with a simple amino acid called D-serine improved memory and learning, offering a potential new approach to age-related cognitive decline.

item.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
item.description: Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden factor that can make or break chemical reactions
item.description: Researchers discovered a hidden factor that can determine whether chemical reactions succeed or fail, and then used it to boost the proportion of the desired product from 16% to 97%. By controlling acidity near electrodes, they developed a promising way to manufacture chemicals for plastics, medicines, and other products using oxygen and electricity instead of hazardous added oxidants.

item.title: Scientists discover vanilla’s hidden healing potential
item.description: Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine.

item.title: Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep
item.description: Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, while even light activities like walking and standing breaks were linked to better sleep and mood.

item.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

item.title: The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments
item.description: Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimer’s disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation.

item.title: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life.

item.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
item.description: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.

item.title: New injection makes fat cells self-destruct
item.description: Scientists have developed an experimental injection that destroys fat cells and significantly reduces dangerous belly fat, potentially opening a new path to treating obesity. Early research also suggests it could help prevent the weight regain that often follows stopping popular weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy.

item.title: The eye has a hidden cleanup system scientists never knew existed
item.description: Scientists have discovered a hidden cleanup system at the back of the eye that drains fluid and waste through a previously unknown pathway. The surprising finding, demonstrated in mice, could open the door to new treatments for glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other causes of blindness.

item.title: Eating olive oil before carbs has a surprising effect on blood sugar
item.description: A simple change in the order you eat your food could help prevent blood sugar spikes. Scientists discovered that giving mice olive oil before carbohydrates slowed digestion and activated a surprising combination of hormones and nerve signals that helped regulate blood sugar, even in mice with type 2 diabetes.

item.title: Scientists build a nuclear clock that could make atomic clocks obsolete
item.description: Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances.

item.title: A plastic once thought harmless may be fueling fatty liver disease
item.description: One of the world's most common plastics may pose a hidden threat to liver health. Texas A&M researchers discovered that polyethylene microplastics can contribute to fatty liver disease, with potentially worse effects when combined with an unhealthy diet. Even more surprising, this widely used plastic was previously considered relatively harmless.

item.title: Neanderthals may have used prehistoric glue as an ancient antibiotic
item.description: Neanderthals may have used a sticky substance made from birch bark to treat wounds thousands of years before antibiotics existed. Researchers recreated ancient birch tar production techniques and discovered that every sample could inhibit the growth of bacteria responsible for dangerous wound infections. Previously known mainly as a prehistoric glue, birch tar may have doubled as a surprisingly effective natural medicine.

item.title: Scientists created a tiny device that can control your nerves to treat chronic pain
item.description: Scientists have developed a tiny, injectable device that can control nerve activity without surgery, batteries, or wires, potentially transforming treatment for chronic pain and movement disorders. Powered wirelessly from outside the body, the seed-sized technology has shown promising results in early testing.

item.title: A surprisingly simple way to relieve knee arthritis pain without pills or surgery
item.description: A surprisingly simple change in how you walk could help relieve knee arthritis pain and even slow joint damage. In a year-long clinical trial, researchers found that adjusting the angle of a person's foot while walking reduced osteoarthritis pain by an amount comparable to medication, without requiring drugs or surgery. Even more promising, MRI scans revealed that participants who adopted the personalized walking technique experienced slower deterioration in a marker of knee cartilage health.

item.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
item.description: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

item.title: NASA astronauts splash down after 100 million miles in space
item.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have returned to Earth after 237 days in space, traveling more than 100 million miles and completing over 3,792 orbits while conducting research to prepare for future missions to the Moon and Mars. The mission also made history with record-setting spacewalk achievements and experiments that could transform medicine both in space and on Earth.

item.title: October’s night sky is full of cosmic tricks and treats
item.description: October’s skies are packed with celestial surprises, from Jupiter disappearing behind the Moon to two meteor showers lighting up the darkness. NASA highlights four must-see events, including shooting stars from Halley’s Comet and a glowing Hunter’s Moon just before Halloween.

item.title: NASA is searching for hidden caves to build its first Moon base
item.description: NASA is preparing for humanity’s first Moon base with three investigations that will hunt for underground shelters, uncover hidden ice, and track dangerous conditions on the lunar surface. The findings could reveal how astronauts can survive and thrive on the Moon while laying the groundwork for future journeys to Mars.
